body.p: In view of the claim amendments and below remarks, the Examiner is respectfully requested to reconsider the rejections. The Applicant thanks the Examiner for the determination of allowable subject matter.
Office Action Summary

Claims 16-20 and 37 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian et al., (US20170097413A1) in view of Griesdorf et al., (US9989622B1) and in further view of Stivoric et al., (US20170156594A1), Rogers (US20170351827A1), and Kate (US20200066130A1).

Claim 21 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate as applied to claim 18, and further in view of Hauenstein et al., (US20170095181A1), (hereinafter "Hauenstein").

Claim 23 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate as applied to claim 18, and further in view of Sun et al., (US20120203491A1) (hereinafter "Sun") and Komaromi et al., (US20160162256A1) (hereinafter "Komaromi").

Claim 24 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate as applied to claim 16, and further in view of Alsheikh et al. (M. A. Alsheikh, S. Lin, D. Niyato and H. -P. Tan, "Machine Learning in Wireless Sensor Networks: Algorithms, Strategies, and Applications," in IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, vol. 16, no. 4, pp. 1996-2018, Fourth quarter 2014, doi: 10.1 109/COMST.2014.2320099) and Simpson et al., (US20190336107A1).

Claim 25 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate as applied to claim 20, and further in view Kim et al., "Tracking a Moving Target with Multipole Doppler Sensors Using an Artificial Neural Network", IEEE Antennas and Propagation Society International Symposium, June 9-15, pp. 1477-1480,
(hereinafter "Kim") and Rogers.
Claim 26 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate as applied to claim 17, and further in view of Sun and Komaromi.
Claims 27-30 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian in view of Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate.
Claim 32 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate applied to claim 31, and further in view of Hauenstein.

Claim 33 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rodgers, Kate, and Hauenstein applied to claim 32, and further in view of DeLuca et al., (US6238338B1).

Claim 34 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate, applied to claim 27, and further in view Yuen et al., (US 20190186949 Al).
Claim 35 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate.

A rationale for the rejection of claim 31 is not provided within the Office Action, even though on page 26 of the Office Action the Examiner indicates that claim 31 is rejected over Gillian as modified by Griesdorf, Stivoric, Rogers, and Kate.

Claims 22 and 36 were objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
The Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Section 103,
because the prior art does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of the independent claims. MPEP 2143.03 (all claim limitations must be considered).

1. Independent claims 16, 27, 35: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein an amount of time between when native sensor data representative of activity of a user that is associated with a second apparatus comprising a health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application using a first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of time
Independent claim 16 has been amended for clarification to claim (independent claims 27 and 35 have been amended similarly):
"wherein an amount of time between when the native sensor data representative of

the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of
time."
Support for this amendment is within the filed specification at page 4, line 35 to page 5, line 8 and FIG. 1 (item 104).

Kate paragraph [0019] (corresponding to paragraph [0016] of Kate's priority application, namely EP application number 17169013.4 filed May 2, 2017, hereinafter "Kate's priority application") describes that a processor is configured to identify, based on a first set of one or more signals indicative of detected activity of a subject in a first area, a first point in time after cessation of the detected activity in the first area by a predetermined time interval, and that the first point in time corresponds to a subject in a sleep state. Kate's priority application describes at paragraph [0016] that the first set of one or more signals is received from a first sensor.

Kate paragraph [0019] describes that the processor is further configured to identify, based on a second set of one or more signals indicative of activity of the subject in a second area that is different from the first area, a second point in time that is after the first point in time, and that if the first set of signals provided any signals indicative of activity detected in the first area within a second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time, the processor is configured to store an indication of a transition of the subject into an awake state, and that if the first set of signals did not provide any signals indicative of activity detected in the first area within the second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time, the processor refrains from storing the indication of the transition of the subject into an awake state. Kate's priority application describes at paragraph [0016] that the second set of one or more signals is received from a second sensor.

The Examiner stated on pages 6-7 of the Office Action, regarding independent claim 16, that Kate, based on the above-referenced aspects of Kate paragraph [0019], describes the subject matter corresponding to the pre-amended aspect "wherein an amount of time between when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second apparatus or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of time."

The Examiner applies the same rationale to reject the corresponding aspect of independent claim 27 on pages 24-25 of the Office Action, and the corresponding aspect of independent claim 35 on pages 35-36 of the Office Action.

However, Kate at best describes determining a first point in time based on a received first set of one or more signals, and a second point in time after the first point in time, where the second point in time is determined based on a received second set of one or more signals. Kate however does not describe that a time between when the first set of one or more signals is not provided or is not available, and when the second set of one or more signals is received, is less than a threshold amount of time.

Kate describes a first case (Case 1) where, if the first set of signals provided any signals indicative of activity detected in the first area within the second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time, the processor is configured to store an indication that signifies a transition of the subject into a second state, wherein the second state is an awake state. This first case may be illustrated as follows:

As can be seen above, in the first case, 1) the first set of signals from the first sensor are provided within the predetermined time interval (e.g. to determine whether or not there is a cessation of activity), and 2) the first set of signals from the first sensor are still provided within second time interval. Kate does not describe that the first set of signals have stopped being provided or are unavailable within either of the predetermined time interval or the second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time.

Kate describes a second case (Case 2) where, if the first set of signals did not provide any signals indicative of activity detected in the first area within the second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time, the processor is configured to refrain from storing the indication that signifies a transition of the subject into the second awake state.
This second case may be illustrated as follows:

As can be seen above, similar to the first case, in the second case, 1) the first set of signals from the first sensor are provided within the predetermined time interval (e.g. to determine whether or not there is a cessation of activity), and 2) the first set of signals from the first sensor are still provided within second time interval. Kate merely describes that in the second case, the first set of signals did not provide any signals indicative of activity detected in the first area within the second time interval. However, Kate does not describe that the first set of signals have stopped being provided or are unavailable within either of the predetermined time interval or the second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time. For example, the first set of signals may provide signals indicative of no activity detected in the first area within the second time interval (e.g. signals received by bed area sensor 106 detects no activity near bed 104 in bedroom 102 (due to the subject sleeping), and signals received by hallway sensor 110 detects no activity in hallway 108).

In contrast, in Applicant's case, Applicant claims that the time between when the native sensor data is not provided or is unavailable, and when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided, is less than a threshold amount of time.
This may be illustrated as follows:

As can be seen above, the native sensor data is not being provided during the time interval that represents a threshold amount of time (the native sensor data associated with the second apparatus stops being provided or is unavailable at the beginning of the time interval).

It would be understood by a person skilled in the art, that in case 2 described by Kate, the first set of signals not providing any signals indicative of activity detected in the first area within the second time interval immediately preceding the second point in time means that the first set of signals did not provide signals indicative of not sleeping in the first area, where the first set of signals provides signals indicative of sleeping (the first set of signals are still being provided). In contrast, in Applicant's case, when the native sensor data stops being provided the native sensor data stops providing signals indicative of both sleeping and not sleeping (native sensor data is not being provided at all).

That the first set of signals are still being provided throughout the duration of the activity or inactivity of the user is further depicted in Fig. 4 of Kate and Kate's priority application. Kate paragraph [0064] describes "As shown by the plots and circular endpoints, in day 1, the subject slept for a relatively long first period, got out of bed briefly before returning to bed

for a second slightly shorter period of sleep, and then left bed once more before getting back into bed for a third period of sleep. In day 2 the subject went to sleep somewhat later than in day 1 but only left bed once between periods of sleep. In day three the subject exhibited sleeping patterns similar to those of day 1, except that the subject collectively slept longer."
Fig. 4 of Kate is shown below:
In Kate, the first set of signals are provided throughout the entire duration of the tracking period.
Whereas in Applicant's case, the pseudo sensor data is provided in response to the native sensor data not being provided or being unavailable, as demonstrated by Applicant's FIG. 3B.
Applicant's FIG. 3B is shown below:

Such an implementation detail is described within Applicant's filed specification at page 8, lines 11-17 which describes (bolding added) "However, if there is a time during which the sensor 399 cannot generate sensor data (e.g., due to charging or for other reasons as noted), this time may be considered a gap in the continuous stream of sensor data. In some embodiments, the gap may be defined by a predefined time where there is no sensor data, such as 2 minutes (although other times may be used as well), while in some embodiments, the gap may be defined by a message or trigger signal indicating that the sensor 399 is not able to generate sensor data."
Such an embodiment, where a time between when sensor data associated with a second
apparatus is not provided or is unavailable, and when pseudo sensor data is provided, is less than a threshold amount of time is not disclosed or suggested by the prior art including Kate.

Also, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Kate with the other references to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention. Paragraph [0006] of Kate is cited by the Examiner on pages 7, 25, and 36 of the Office Action for the motivation to combine Kate within the Office Action on pages )

Even though Kate at paragraph [0006] (corresponding to paragraph [0005] of Kate's priority application) describes "a need to accurately and unobtrusively monitor subjects in their living environment," in Kate and Kate's priority application, the first set of signals received from the first sensor are not derived using artificial intelligence or machine learning, and the second set of signals received from the second sensor are not derived using artificial intelligence or machine learning. The terms "artificial intelligence" and "machine learning" do not appear in Kate or in Kate's priority application. In Applicant's claims, the pseudo sensor data is derived using the first apparatus based on at least a machine learning model configured to transform the radio frequency based data into the pseudo sensor data.

In addition, Kate does not describe that the second set of signals are provided due to the first set of signals not being provided. For this reason, Kate does not disclose new claim 38, which claims (bolding added) "wherein the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker due to the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application not being provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application or the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user being unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application." Support for new claim 38 is within the filed specification at page 1, line 38 to page 2, line 4.

Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest "wherein an amount of time between when native sensor data representative of activity of a user that is associated with a second apparatus comprising a health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second

apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application using a first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of time." Independent claim 16, on the other hand, claims (with similar subject matter being recited in independent claims 27 and 35), "wherein an amount of time between when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user that is associated with the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application begins to not be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application or when the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user begins to be unavailable to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application, and when the pseudo sensor data begins to be provided to the second apparatus comprising the health or fitness tracker application using the first apparatus comprising the radio frequency based tracker, is less than a threshold amount of time." This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 16, 27, and 35 are patentable and should be allowed.
2. Even if it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above

Applicant respectfully traverses the rationale to combine the references to support a rejection under Section 103, because one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Kate with the other references to arrive at Applicant's claims invention. Paragraph [0006] of Kate is cited by the Examiner on pages 7, 25, and 36 of the Office Action for the motivation to combine Kate with the other references.

As mentioned above within Point 1, even though Kate at paragraph [0006] (corresponding to paragraph [0005] of Kate's priority application) describes "a need to accurately and unobtrusively monitor subjects in their living environment," in Kate and Kate's priority application, the first set of signals received from the first sensor are not derived using artificial intelligence or machine learning, and the second set of signals received from the second sensor are not derived using artificial intelligence or machine learning. The terms "artificial intelligence" and "machine learning" do not appear in Kate or in Kate's priority application. In Applicant's
claims, the pseudo sensor data is derived using the first apparatus based on at least a machine learning model configured to transform the radio frequency based data into the pseudo sensor data.

Even if, for the sake of argument, it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims as a whole, as explained above. When applying Section 103 to Applicant's claimed invention, the claimed invention should be considered as a whole per Hodosh v. Block Drug Co., Inc., 786 F.2d 1136, 1143 n.5 (Fed. Cir. 1986) ("when applying § 103: (1) the claimed invention must be considered as a whole").
3. Other dependent claims

Though the other dependent claims contain their own allowable subject matter, these claims should at least be allowable due to their dependence from allowable independent claims. However, to expedite prosecution at this time, no further comment will be made.

The Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner enter this amendment and pass the claims to issue. The undersigned representative welcomes the opportunity to resolve any matters that may remain, formal or otherwise, via teleconference at the Examiner's discretion.
